A2.text:
When Aysel's grandfather died, she inherited his old gramophone. It was big, dusty and very heavy. For two years, it stood in the corner of her flat. “Old things only gather dust,” her brother Elvin said. “Sell it. It is old junk. Buy something new.”

Aysel took it to an antique shop on Nizami Street. The man looked at it. “It is vintage, but it is broken,” he said. “It is not worth much. I can give you fifty manats.”

Aysel did not sell it. She wanted to restore it. She watched videos and bought a small second-hand part online. It took her three weekends.

Finally, the gramophone worked! Aysel opened the little drawer under it. Inside, she found an old record with no name.

She played it. First there was noise. Then she heard a young man singing an old Azerbaijani love song. It was her grandfather! He recorded it for her grandmother in 1965.

Aysel cried. She called Elvin. He came and listened with her. He was quiet for a long time.

“I'm sorry,” he said. “It is not junk. It is a keepsake.”

Aysel smiled. “One man's trash is another man's treasure,” she said. “This gramophone can stand the test of time — and Grandpa's song too.”

B1.text:
When Aysel's grandfather passed away, the family divided his things quickly. Her brother Elvin took the car, her cousins took the carpets, and Aysel, who arrived last, inherited what nobody else wanted: a huge wooden gramophone cabinet from the 1960s.

For two years it stood in the corner of her small flat, gathering dust.

“Just sell it,” Elvin said every time he visited. “It's an ugly piece of junk taking up half your living room.”

Eventually, she carried it in a taxi to an antique dealer near Fountain Square. He lifted the lid, turned the handle and shook his head. “Vintage, yes. Valuable, no. The motor's dead, the needle's gone. Honestly, it's not worth more than sixty manats.”

Something in Aysel refused. Instead of selling it, she decided to restore it herself. She watched hours of videos, cleaned forty years of dust from the inside and ordered a second-hand motor from a collector in Ganja. It took four weekends and two cut fingers.

On the fifth Saturday, the turntable began to spin. Aysel was so happy she laughed out loud. Then she noticed a small drawer at the bottom of the cabinet that she had never opened. Inside was a single black record in a paper cover, with a date written by hand: “12.05.1965.”

She put it on. After a few seconds of crackling, a young man's voice began to sing an old Azerbaijani love song, slightly out of tune but full of feeling. Aysel knew the voice immediately. It was her grandfather, at twenty-two, singing for the girl who would become her grandmother.

She called Elvin. He came over without asking why and listened, standing very still. When the song finished, he sat down heavily on the sofa.

“I was wrong,” he said quietly. “This isn't junk. It's the best keepsake any of us got.”

Aysel put the record back in its paper cover. “One man's trash is another man's treasure,” she said. “Some things just stand the test of time.”

B2.text:
When Aysel's grandfather died, his belongings were divided with brisk efficiency. Her brother Elvin claimed the car, her cousins the carpets, and Aysel, arriving last from a business trip, inherited the one item nobody else had wanted: a hulking walnut gramophone cabinet from the 1960s.

For two years it occupied a corner of her small flat, quietly gathering dust and serving as a shelf for her houseplants.

“Sell the thing,” Elvin urged at every visit. “It's a monstrous piece of junk that's eating half your living room.”

Eventually she wrestled it into a taxi and delivered it to an antique dealer near Fountain Square. He raised the lid, cranked the handle and sighed. “Vintage, certainly. Valuable, no. Dead motor, missing needle. Frankly, it isn't worth more than sixty manats.”

Something in Aysel dug in its heels. Rather than sell it, she resolved to restore it herself. She absorbed hours of tutorials, removed four decades of grime from its interior and tracked down a second-hand motor from a collector in Ganja. The project consumed four weekends and cost her two cut fingers.

On the fifth Saturday, the turntable began to revolve, and she laughed aloud in the empty flat. It was only then that she noticed a shallow drawer at the base of the cabinet that she had never thought to open. Inside lay a single black record in a paper sleeve, a date pencilled on it by hand: “12.05.1965.”

She lowered the needle. After a few seconds of crackle, a young man's voice rose into a traditional Azerbaijani love song — not quite in tune, but trembling with feeling. She recognised it instantly. It was her grandfather, aged twenty-two, serenading the girl who would one day become her grandmother.

She rang Elvin. He arrived without asking why and stood motionless through the entire song. When the last note faded, he lowered himself onto the sofa.

“I was wrong,” he said, barely above a whisper. “It's not junk. It's the most precious keepsake any of us received.”

Aysel slid the record back into its sleeve. “One man's trash is another man's treasure,” she said softly. “And some things stand the test of time far better than we do.”
